text:
The rain lashed against the precinct windows, mirroring the storm brewing in Detective Howard’s chest. It was his last day. The retirement party was scheduled for 8:00 AM, complete with a cake and a speech about loyalty. But at 6:00 AM, he had found the ledger.

It wasn’t just evidence; it was a confession written in blood and ink, implicating his partner, Marcus, in the very corruption case they had spent five years dismantling. The irony was a physical weight in Howard’s gut. He had trusted Marcus with his life, with his back, and now, apparently, with his soul.

Howard sat in his dimly lit office, the ledger open before him. His hand hovered over the phone that would call Internal Affairs. If he made the call, Marcus would be arrested before the cake was even cut. Their thirty-year friendship would end in handcuffs. If he didn’t, he was complicit. He was no longer a detective; he was an accessory.

The door creaked open. Marcus stood there, holding two coffees, his face bright with the naive optimism of a man who believed the world was still black and white. "Hey, old friend," Marcus said, smiling. "Ready to hang up the gun?"

Howard looked at the man he called brother, then at the ledger. The tension in the room spiked, thick and suffocating. Howard’s heart hammered against his ribs, a frantic drumbeat counting down the seconds until his choice would become irreversible. He couldn't speak. He couldn't breathe. The loyalty he thought was unshakable was cracking, and with it, the foundation of his entire life.

"Howard?" Marcus’s smile faltered, sensing the shift in the air. "You okay? You look like you’ve seen a ghost."

Howard closed the ledger slowly, the sound like a gunshot in the quiet room. "I’m fine, Marcus," he lied, his voice steady despite the chaos within. "Just thinking about what comes next."

But as Marcus set the coffee down, his eyes drifted to the open drawer where the ledger lay half-hidden. The color drained from Marcus’s face. The trust was gone, replaced by a cold, hard fear. The game had changed, and Howard was no longer just retiring; he was hunting.
